transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-16 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~52 minutes | Recording: On
Attendees: Riley N., Avery C., Diego M., Sofia P. (Redwood); Dr. Priya R., Marcus E., Talia B., Evan C. (Lumina)
Summary: A conversational customer interview (fireside style) focused on Lumina's journey adopting Redwood for clinical natural language processing, cost/perf outcomes, and a few technical anecdotes for a customer-focused case study.
Topics: intro and context; why Redwood; results (latency, cost, accuracy); deployment story (private vs hosted); security/compliance notes; anecdotes; CTA + next steps.

00:00 - Riley: "Hey everyone, welcome and thanks for joining our fireside chat. I'm Riley from Redwood, and with me are Avery and Diego, and Sofia who's recording. Priya, Marcus, thanks so much for making time. Do you want to kick off with a quick intro of Lumina?"

00:23 - Dr. Priya: "Yeah, thanks Riley — really excited. So quick snapshot: Lumina builds clinical NLP models that extract structured insights from doctor notes and pathology reports. We've been around for 6 years, the ML stack's... it's a mix of in-house models and open foundation models for augmentation. We work with three large hospital systems and a few specialty clinics."

01:05 - Marcus: "We were facing scale issues — the model was fine in a notebook but when we tried streaming inference into EHR workflows, cost and latency were a problem, and compliance is huge for us. So we started piloting Redwood in Q1 this year."

01:40 - Avery: "For the audience, what was the timeline — discovery, pilot, rollout?"

01:47 - Dr. Priya: "Discovery in January, pilot in March, canary with one hospital in May, full rollout in July. So fairly fast. The pilot was critical because we needed to validate both performance and that logs and PHI handling matched our security remit."

02:15 - Diego: "Nice — can you share the big 'before vs after' numbers you found? We like real numbers, always help folks relate."

02:24 - Evan: "Yeah sure. For our chief extraction pipeline, before Redwood on our self-managed endpoints average P95 latency at 512 tokens was about 720ms; on Redwood hosted with the Dedicated offering we got that down to 210ms P95. Cost per 1k requests dropped by roughly 48% when accounting for better batching and prefix caching. Accuracy on the downstream entity linking was unchanged — within noise, 0.5% delta — which was important."

03:10 - Sofia: "That's a big delta. Marcus, any notes on infra ops overhead?"

03:18 - Marcus: "Oh yeah. Before: we were running a small MLOps team handling autoscaling, kernel selection, and tuning. After Redwood, the day-to-day infra ops hours went down by around 30% according to our internal tracking — fewer incidents, fewer hotfix cycles."

03:45 - Riley: "There's often a worry about handing over control. How did your engineers feel about black box trade-offs?"

03:53 - Dr. Priya: "Initially skeptical. We insisted on a Private deployment pattern — VPC with customer-managed KMS — so logs and keys stayed in our environment. That convinced the security folks. Also, Diego ran a few microbenchmarks comparing different quantization profiles; Redwood's SE helped interpret the numbers which made us comfortable."

04:30 - Diego: "Quick sidebar: do you recall any gotchas in the private setup?"

04:36 - Evan: "Yeah one small networking thing — our egress rules were too strict, so the control plane couldn't pull a small helper image. Turned out to be a corporate firewall rule. Took a morning to debug. But once we sorted it, the deployment was stable."

05:05 - Avery: "This is great for a case study — can you share a short anecdote about a piece of product feedback that came from using Redwood?"

05:12 - Dr. Priya: "Sure — we noticed that when clinicians pasted long notes the latency spiked unexpectedly. Redwood's prefix caching suggestion meant that many common headers and templates were cached across requests, which dropped tail latency a lot. That was an easy win in production and the clinicians noticed the UI felt snappier."

05:48 - Riley: "Nice. On the metrics side, did you instrument Redwood Console dashboards? Was it useful for troubleshooting?"

05:55 - Marcus: "Very useful. We used the per-token cost breakdown to justify billing allocations to product teams, and tracing hooks helped correlate spikes to a recent model rollout — we rolled back via canary and the problem disappeared."

06:30 - Diego: "Any comments on quality regression monitoring or evals? This is often overlooked in marketing stories but is real operational work."

06:38 - Evan: "We hooked up Redwood's eval pipeline to run nightly checks on a small corpus of gold prompts. It flagged a small regression after a model swap. With that alert we rolled a quick rollback which avoided customer-facing issues. So monitoring paid for itself."

07:05 - Sofia: "Listeners love the human side — what did product teams think about adopting the Redwood API? Was onboarding smooth?"

07:12 - Dr. Priya: "Actually onboarding was smooth. The SDK snippets worked, but the best part was the 'model variant' docs — we could pin variants per workflow. That saved us from building an in-house router initially."

07:40 - Riley: "There's always the question of vendor lock-in. Did you build a fallback plan?"

07:47 - Marcus: "Yes — we maintain a small fallback path to run a quantized local replica for critical low-volume calls. But mostly we trust Redwood and the routing fallback features have been solid."

08:10 - Avery: "Switching gears — compliance. Social proof is important for other hospitals. Any notes on audits or attestation?"

08:20 - Dr. Priya: "Redwood's SOC 2 docs and audit logs were helpful. We went through a third-party audit for one of our enterprise customers and Redwood's logs helped provide evidence for request handling and data retention. We also used SSO with SAML for segmenting team access."

08:50 - Riley: "Nice. We get asked a lot about data residency — did that come up?"

08:56 - Marcus: "For some partners yes. We used Redwood Private deployments in a region to satisfy data residency needs. That capability was the main gating factor for one hospital contract."

09:20 - Diego: "Can you share a short story where cost/perf tradeoff mattered to clinical outcomes?"

09:29 - Dr. Priya: "There was a pilot where we had to surface urgent flags in triage — if the NLP latency was too high, triage nurses wouldn't wait. After the Redwood rollout, the faster P95 meant more flags were surfaced in the triage UI within the required timeout window, which led to earlier clinician followups in at least three cases we tracked. That was concrete impact."

10:05 - Sofia: "Powerful. A few audience Qs we pulled beforehand — first: 'How much effort to switch models or update prompts at scale?'"

10:15 - Evan: "We use a small prompts repo and Redwood supports parameterized prompts and function-calls which made it manageable. Rolling prompts via Canary was straightforward."

10:40 - Riley: "Next question: 'Did you have to retrain models or mostly rely on zero-shot/few-shot with the open models?'

10:48 - Dr. Priya: "A mix. For entity extraction we still train bespoke models, but for summarization and clinical note normalization we use fine-tuned open models and Redwood hosted models for inference — the runtime handles the heavy lifting."

11:20 - Diego: "A slightly nerdy one: any kernel/quantization tradeoffs you recall?"

11:26 - Evan: "Diego, you're gonna laugh — we tried a 4-bit quantized path and saw minor throughput gains but a small OR drop on rare entities. We ended up using 8-bit for production. Redwood's kernel selection helped test those quickly."

11:55 - Marcus: "There's some art here — you tune for the worst-case clinical query, not the average one."

12:10 - Avery: "Let's do a quick lightning round of 'advice to other healthcare startups' — one sentence each?"

12:17 - Dr. Priya: "Prioritize security in pilot planning; it's harder to bolt on later."

12:23 - Marcus: "Measure tail latency early — P95 matters more than P50 in clinical apps."

12:28 - Evan: "Keep a lightweight fallback path even if you trust the vendor."

12:34 - Riley: "Sofia?"

12:36 - Sofia: "Document prompts and evals; they save you later."

12:42 - Riley: "Okay, moving toward closing — any fun anecdote about clinicians reacting?"

12:49 - Dr. Priya: "One clinician thought the notes summary was 'scary accurate' and joked we were reading minds — she then spent a week finding tiny edge cases to stump us, which was actually helpful."

13:05 - Avery: "Great quote. We'll use that with approval. Speaking of approvals, Priya, Marcus — can you sign off on a short pull quote about latency and clinical impact?"

13:16 - Dr. Priya: "Yes, happy to. We'll get the quote back by next Friday. Keep it short, like two sentences."

13:25 - Riley: "Perfect. A few technical listeners will want more — Diego and Evan will do a 30–45 minute deep-dive on October 6th — we'll put calendar invites. Any final thoughts?"

13:40 - Marcus: "Thanks — this was fun. For folks building models for healthcare: focus on operationalizing quality, not just model metrics."

13:55 - Riley: "Thank you all. We'll follow up with artifacts: the edited clip, the transcript, and a short case study draft. Anything else to add?"

14:05 - Dr. Priya: "Nope, thanks. Appreciate the collaboration — the Redwood SEs were a huge help."

14:14 - Sofia: "End recording."

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings — examples include 'K-V casse' (should be KV cache), 'SOS two' (SOC 2), and some speaker labels condensed to initials. We preserved some filler and overlapping talk to keep the dialog natural.

References shared during call: https://redwood.ai/case-studies/lumina (draft link), internal benchmark sheet (shared in chat), SOC 2 attestation (link provided by Redwood SE).

Recap (for editorial use):
- Headline metric: P95 latency improvement from ~720ms -> ~210ms on Dedicated; ~48% cost reduction per 1k requests after batching/caching.
- Primary value props used: Dedicated capacity, VPC/private deployment, prefix/KV caching, Redwood Console observability, model variant rollouts.
- Human impact anecdote: faster triage flags led to earlier clinician followups in tracked cases.

End of transcript.
